Abstract

Acknowledgements: We thank the Kleine Weltentdecker*innen Lab and the Jacobs Center for Productive Youth Development at Universität Zürich for providing the resources necessary to this research and all children and their caregivers for their participation in our studies. Next to that, we want to thank Chiara Carrel and Merve Bot for their effort and contribution to the project. This work was partially funded by the Jacobs Foundation. We would like to thank both reviewers for their helpful commentary, and in particular Reviewer 1 for helpful suggestions on how the study's results could be used to extend the Dual-Process Perspective on over-imitation.

The Influence of Parental Cultural Values on Preschool Children's Over-Imitation

Imitation is one of the most important learning avenues for humans. It is fundamental to our species' ability to accumulate culture across generations (Heyes, 2001). Imitation is defined by copying the actions or behaviours of an observed model (Legare & Nielsen, 2015). Children use imitation in everyday life and at various levels (Heyes, 2001; Nielsen & Tomaselli, 2010): it underlies their acquisition of motor actions and practical skills (Ledford & Wolery, 2011), instrumental tool use (Legare & Nielsen, 2015), language (Klinger et al., 2016), and the transmission of customs and norms (Over & Carpenter, 2013). This makes it a vital part of early development (Carpenter & Nielsen, 2008). Given the importance of imitation to our species and to individual development, researchers strive to explain how and when it emerges, and under what circumstances.

Over-imitation

Imitation also occurs when we are not explicitly trying to achieve a certain goal.

Humans tend to imitate others' behaviour, even when their goal is unclear. This phenomenon is known as over-imitation (Hoehl et al., 2019) and is observed in both children and adults (Horner & Whiten, 2005; McGuigan et al., 2011 McGuigan et al., , 2012)).

Over-imitation has been reported across different cultures, although its extent varies (Nielsen & Tomaselli, 2010; Stengelin et al., 2020). For instance, children from more collectivistic cultural backgrounds over-imitate more than children from individualistic ones (Clegg & Legare, 2016; Fong et al., 2021), and over-imitation rates differ between Western, first nation, and Bushmen children (Nielsen et al., 2014), which we discuss in detail below.

To study over-imitation, participants, usually children, observe a series of unnecessary actions followed by a single action necessary to achieve a goal. After this observation phase, they are given the opportunity to act independently. Over-imitation is evident in children's performance of unnecessary actions, and how many of these are performed varies systematically across individuals and contexts (Hoehl et al., 2019). A common paradigm to study over-imitation involves retrieving a reward from an object, such as a puzzle box (Horner & Whiten, 2005), although paradigms vary widely and include, for instance, imitation of unnecessary steps in everyday tasks and social interactions (Legare & Nielsen, 2015).

The mechanisms underlying over-imitation can be grouped into causal, affiliative, and normative processes (Hoehl et al., 2019). Causal processes occur when people assume that others' actions have a purpose, even if this purpose is unclear to them. These are supported by findings that children selectively omit accidental actions (Gardiner, 2014; Lyons et al., 2011) and are sensitive to whether a model acts intentionally (Gergely et al., 2002). Affiliative processes occur when people copy others' actions because they want to affiliate with them, as imitation can signal social alignment and strengthen interpersonal bonds. Children over-imitate more, when a familiar, in-group model demonstrates actions (Buttelmann et al., 2013; Nielsen & Blank, 2011) and when they are being observed (Stengelin et al., 2019). Normative explanations propose that individuals treat demonstrated actions as socially prescribed, assuming that even unnecessary steps are part of the social norms -a conventional or "correct" behaviour. For example, not only do children reproduce unnecessary actions themselves, but they also expect third parties to do so and protest when they do not (Kenward, 2012; Keupp et al., 2013). All three processes have been systematically shown to be involved in why we over-imitate (Hoehl et al., 2019).

For instance, children do not imitate irrelevant actions that are accidental or unintentional (Gardiner, 2014; Lyons et al., 2011), suggesting they actively infer intent. For intentional actions, children still over-imitate even when they are not being observed and are explicitly told they will get a reward regardless (Hoehl et al., 2014; Schleihauf et al., 2018), or when they are unaware of participating in an experiment at all (Whiten et al., 2016). These findings suggest that over-imitation reflects an interaction between cognitive inference, social motivation, and sensitivity to cultural norms.

The Development of Over-imitation

Age-related changes influence the extent to which children reproduce irrelevant actions. In the second year of life, children do not yet over-imitate, but they are already selective in their copying of others' behaviour: They imitate models differently based on their group membership (Buttelmann et al., 2013), confidence (Birch et al., 2010), age (Zmyj, Aschersleben, et al., 2012; Zmyj, Daum, et al., 2012), competence (Crivello et al., 2018; Zmyj et al., 2010), the inferred rationality of others' actions (Gergely & Csibra, 2003; Gergely et al., 2002), the salience of context stimuli (Beisert et al., 2012), and their motor resonance (Paulus et al., 2011, mapping others' actions onto their own motor repertoire).

A developmental shift occurs in the second year of infants' lives, as they become increasingly likely to copy others' actions regardless of their causal relevance (Brugger et al., 2007; Gellén & Buttelmann, 2019; Hilbrink et al., 2013). Children's over-imitation increases between the ages of 3 and 8 (Stengelin et al., 2019). Clay et al. (2018) showed with 4-to 6-year-old children that these age-related changes in over-imitation likely reflect the changing underlying processes. Younger children were more likely to over-imitate when the unnecessary actions were framed as instrumental (causally relevant), whereas older children were more likely to over-imitate when the unnecessary actions were framed as normative. In addition, younger children were more likely to reproduce the actions performed on or in contact with the puzzle box rather than other actions, compared to older children, likely because they perceive object-bound actions as more causally relevant (Clay et al., 2018). This demonstrates that with age, the relative importance of the mechanisms underlying over-imitation changes: children's tendency to over-imitate increasingly reflects sensitivity to the social (Nielsen & Blank, 2011) and normative context of the demonstration (Kenward, 2012) rather than assumptions about causality. Therefore, children's growing understanding of social conventions and their increasing awareness of others' expectations increase the role of normative and affiliative motivations for over-imitation with age.

Dual-Process Perspective

Early theoretical accounts of over-imitation stress its two main functions: instrumental (to learn something new; Lyons et al., 2007 Lyons et al., , 2011;; Whiten et al., 2009) and social (to affiliate or adhere to social norms; Over & Carpenter, 2013). The dual-process perspective on over-imitation aims to unify those explanations, and place them in the context of children's development (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020). It explains over-imitation behaviour of children in different contexts and situations. Whether children over-imitate or not is based on the interaction between two distinct types of processing: type 1 and type 2. Blanket copying, based on type 1 processing, is quick and low in cognitive effort. It occurs when children imitate others' unnecessary actions without explicitly questioning their causal relevance or motivation. Under certain circumstances, blanket copying can be overridden when children are prompted to question whether demonstrated actions are necessary. In such cases, children engage in deliberate considerations of whether or not to copy, based on type 2 processing, which is slower and requires more cognitive effort.

Type 2 processing is triggered when the observer recognises that the actions he or she observed were causally irrelevant. This can happen in a number of ways: by observing an efficient strategy after seeing a demonstration that included unnecessary actions, or by observing actions that did not involve contact with the puzzle box (non-contact actions, e.g. clapping), which are clearly recognisable as causally irrelevant. In contrast, observing pseudo-instrumental actions (actions that look instrumental, but are not; e.g., pressing a button) is more likely to lead to type 1 processing because they can be easily mistaken for instrumental actions. To sum up, the dual-process perspective on over-imitation posits that observation of unnecessary actions might lead to either type 1 or type 2 processing, depending on the context and the types of actions being observed. Triggering children's type 2 processing leads to deliberate considerations whether or not to copy (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020). Different factors might influence this consideration at different levels. External factors such as demonstration context (e.g., instrumental or normative instructions; Legare et al., 2015), setting, such as the environment (e.g., experimental or natural setting; Whiten et al., 2016), or others' behaviour (e.g., being observed or not; Marsh et al., 2019) may shape the goals children hold in a given situation or interaction. These individual goals (e.g., instrumental, normative, affiliative, or entertainment goals; Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2021) then shape children's decision on whether or not to copy. Individual factors such as personality or personal values (Flynn & Whiten, 2012; Hilbrink et al., 2013)

The Influence of Cultural Values

Over-imitation is a universal phenomenon, but the extent to which children over-imitate differs between cultures (Berl & Hewlett, 2015; Clegg & Legare, 2016; Fong et al., 2021; Nielsen & Tomaselli, 2010; Nielsen et al., 2014; Stengelin et al., 2019 Stengelin et al., , 2020)).

This line of research relied on cross-cultural comparisons. For instance, 6-to 8-year-old children from a Western, individualist culture (United States) over-imitated less than children from a non-Western, collectivist culture (Vanuatu, Melanesian archipelago), when the task was placed in an instrumental, but not normative, context (Clegg & Legare, 2016). Even though the children from both groups were likely able to realise that the unnecessary actions were causally irrelevant, children from a more collectivist culture showed more normative motivation to copy the actions than children from an individualist culture. When the goals of the task were made explicitly normative, children from an individualist culture over-imitated to the same, greater extent as the children from a collectivist culture. Similarly, 4-to 6-year-old children from a rural, indigenous community in Malaysia over-imitated more than children from an urban city in Australia, and a peri-urban township in Malaysia (Fong et al., 2021). This effect was attributed to the stronger conformity preference in the rural community, which increased children's normative goals to copy. Thus, cultural values within children's communities can influence their over-imitation by affecting whether they have normative goals to copy.

The aforementioned studies compared groups defined by geography or ethnicity, leaving open the question of which specific cultural values drive these differences and how they vary at the individual level. The present study addresses this by measuring parents' individual cultural values directly using the GLOBE framework (House et al., 2004). The GLOBE framework assesses nine cultural dimensions, including institutional collectivism (the belief that societal institutions should promote collective action) and in-group collectivism (the belief that families and close groups should be characterised by loyalty and group pride). See Table 1 for definitions and example questions of all nine dimensions assessed.

Prior work showed that institutional collectivism is linked to how children respond to norm violations (Gampe & Daum, 2018): children of parents with higher institutional collectivism responded less saliently to norm violations, suggesting their norm enforcement operates more implicitly. For this reason, we focused in the present study primarily on specific cultural aspects of collectivism. Because over-imitation reflects sensitivity to norms (Kenward, 2012), we expected parents' higher institutional collectivism to be associated with their children's greater over-imitation of actions likely to trigger normative reasoning.

Multicultural and Multilingual Environments

Researchers showing cross-cultural differences in over-imitation in previous studies could only theorise about the reasons responsible for changes in children's behaviour. However, they did not quantify these differences. In addition, through their design, they tested only children embedded in a single culture at a time, assuming a culturally homogeneous environment, even though cultural values differ more strongly between individuals than between countries (Fischer & Schwartz, 2011). Many children, however, grow up in societies that are characterised by cultural, linguistic, and ethnic diversity (Fearon, 2003; Gören, 2013). Even in the European Union and the United States, approximately 25% of children are either born outside their country of residence or have foreign-born parents (Federal Interagency Forum on Child and Family Statistics, 2024; Orav, 2023). These regions are less culturally diverse than regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and southern Asia (Fearon, 2003; Gören, 2013).

Thus, a large portion of children in Western societies grow up with cultural values from multiple cultures. For these children, cultural diversity is therefore not only a societal backdrop but a characteristic of their home environment. Yet, measuring parental cultural values and averaging them into a single score masks the degree to which those values diverge (Smith & Bond, 2019) and thus the diversity in cultural values children experience. Children raised by parents from different cultural backgrounds may experience differing cultural values between their parents. For example, how children react to norm violations is related to culture (Gampe & Daum, 2018). Children from parents with different cultural values, may receive divergent signals about norm violations. This is relevant to over-imitation, because it can be explained by norm learning (Kenward, 2012). The present study, therefore, quantifies the cultural distance between parents as a direct measure of the diversity to which children are exposed at home.

Language and culture are often deeply intertwined (Yagiz & Izadpanah, 2013), and individuals who speak different languages may also hold distinct cultural perspectives and values (Purpuri et al., 2024). In bilingual families (speaking two languages) or bidialectal families (speaking two dialects of the same language), parents often bring different linguistic and cultural backgrounds, which may introduce greater variability in cultural values within the household. Because bilingual children often grow up in more culturally diverse environments than monolingual children, they may more frequently encounter to differing or even conflicting norms, and therefore judge norm violations as less transgressive (Iannuccilli et al., 2021). If bilingual children grow up in households with more divergent cultural values, they may receive more varied normative signals, potentially making them more flexible in their over-imitation.

Bilingualism also affects other, non-imitative, aspects of children's social learning. For instance, bilingual children are better at integrating their interaction partners' visual perspective with their utterances to identify the object being referred to (Yow & Markman, 2015), and at interpreting pointing gestures to clarify ambiguous pronouns (Yow, 2015) and resolve conflicting directional cues (Yow & Markman, 2011).

Therefore, studying children from bilingual families offers a valuable opportunity to measure specific cultural values associated with changes in over-imitation and to disentangle the potential effects of cultural and language diversity.

The Current Study

In the current study, we explored the effect of parents'foot_0 cultural values, the difference in cultural values between parents (as a proxy for cultural diversity), and language status (monolingual/bilingual/bidialectal) on preschool children's over-imitation in a goal-directed task, adopted from Schleihauf et al. (2018). Children between the ages of 3.5 and 4.5 years observed a live demonstration in which an experimenter used a wooden rod to remove a marble from a puzzle box. The demonstration included four causally irrelevant actions followed by the action necessary to retrieve the marble. The unnecessary actions were: clapping (step 1), moving a lever (step 2), tapping the rod in the palm of the hand (step 3), and using the rod to press a button (step 4). Clapping and tapping (steps 1 and 3) can be classified as noncontact, actions, whereas moving a lever and pressing a button (steps 2 and 4) can be classified as pseudo-instrumental (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020). Children were then given an opportunity to interact with the puzzle box themselves, and we measured whether they imitated unnecessary actions (i.e., their over-imitation). In addition, parents completed the GLOBE questionnaire (The Globe Foundation, 2006) to assess their cultural values across nine dimensions (power distance, in-group collectivism, gender egalitarianism, uncertainty avoidance, future orientation, institutional collectivism, performance orientation, humane orientation, and assertiveness; see Table 1, and a questionnaire on the child's language exposure. Cultural diversity was operationalised as the Euclidean distance between the two parents' GLOBE scores across all nine dimensions, capturing the overall degree to which their cultural values diverge.

We combined confirmatory and exploratory approaches. Following the dual-process perspective on over-imitation (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020), we preregistered the prediction that children whose parents endorse greater institutional collectivism are more likely to over-imitate noncontact actions than children whose parents endorse less institutional collectivism. Institutional collectivism refers to the degree to which parents believe that organisational or societal institutions should encourage collective action and the distribution of resources (see Table 1 for all definitions of the assessed cultural domains). We expected to find this effect specifically in noncontact actions because we expected these actions to trigger children's type 2 processing, causing deliberate consideration of whether or not to copy, and thus be affected by children having more normative goals. In contrast, we preregistered the prediction that blanket copying of pseudo-instrumental actions would not be influenced by parental cultural values. We acknowledge that prior work suggests pseudo-instrumental actions may also be modulated by contextual and social factors (Legare & Nielsen, 2015; Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020), but because there is insufficient evidence and no theoretical account directly linking the other cultural dimensions to children's over-imitation, we took an exploratory approach to analyse these associations. In addition, we explored whether children's language status predicted cultural distance between their parents, to assess whether bilingualism is linked to cultural diversity within the family.

Methods

We preregistered the study prior to data analysis (https://osf.io/7ytkd/overview?view_only=d1f9d7b2d08a4a3cb73d2ffdebca4e06 [link for blind peer review, we will share the public link upon acceptance]) and made the collected data and R codes available on the Open Science Framework (see Data Availability Statement). All deviations from the preregistration are explicitly noted.

Participants

We recruited N = 133 children between the ages of 3.5 and 4.5 years (M age = 4.05 years, SD age = 0.29), 48.9% were girls. We chose this age range because four-year-olds are old enough to reliably over-imitate, but young enough that the developmental shift from causal to normative motivations is still ongoing (Clay et al., 2018). This study was also part of a larger project on children's social cognition that targeted that particular age range. Children who were assigned a language status were monolingual Swiss German (n = 41, i.e., not more that 10% input in another language), Swiss German bilingual (n = 44, i.e., at least 20% input in Swiss German and one other language, and not more than 10% input in a third language), or bidialectal (n = 40, i.e., at least 20% input in Swiss German and another variety of German and not more than 10% input in another language/language variety) in accordance with Wermelinger et al. (2017). The language exposure of the other children (n = 8) did not fulfil the requirements to be assigned a specific language status, and they were excluded from the analyses including language status. Bilingual children were exposed to the following languages: English (n = 7), French (n = 5), Spanish (n = 4), Italian (n = 4), Hungarian, Russian, Turkish, Croatian, Portuguese, and Serbian (each n = 2), Icelandic, Greek, Swedish, Norwegian, Finnish, Arabic, Albanian, Mandarin, Tamil, Persian, Polish, and Urdu (each n = 1). Bidialectal children were exposed to the following language varieties: Standard German (n = 38) and Austrian German (n = 2).

Participants were recruited through the research unit's database, which includes of parents who had expressed interest in participating in studies with their children.

Eligible children were healthy, born full-term (gestational age > 37 weeks), had a birth weight above 2500 g, and had no reported diagnoses of developmental disorders, according to parental reports. As compensation, each child received a certificate of participation and a small gift (approximately USD 5,-). Parents provided informed consent for participation. The local Ethics Committee of the university approved the general procedure, which adhered to the ethical standards of the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments. Each session was videotaped and coded from the recording.

Children in our sample predominantly came from families with high socio-economic status. Most participants lived in households with above-average income (Bundesamt fuer Statistik, 2024): 81.2% of parents reported an income higher than the city average, 9.0% reported an income within the average range, and 5.3% reported a below-average income. 4.5% of parents refrained from answering this question. Parental education levels were also high. In 79.7% of households, both parents had completed higher education at a university or a university of applied sciences, while in 15.8% of households, one parent held such a degree. 4.5% of children came from households in which parents had completed other types of education, such as vocational training.

Materials and Design

We used an over-imitation task based on the puzzle box, which consists of a transparent container (as described in Hoehl et al., 2014; Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2021; Schleihauf et al., 2018). Children were presented with a magnetic rod and a transparent Plexiglas container (see Figure 1). Inside the container, a transparent tube held steel marbles. The tube's opening was covered by a lid that could be lifted to allow access to the marbles. The marbles could be retrieved by inserting the magnetic rod into the tube's front opening. A black wooden lever was mounted on top of the box, and a black button enclosed in a transparent square was attached to the bottom right of the container. The transparent design highlighted the irrelevance of certain actions demonstrated during the modelling phase. We used a cross-sectional between-subjects design.

Procedure

The study took place in the lab at the Department of Psychology at the University of Zurich. The language of testing was Swiss German, the societal language.

The experimenter welcomed the children and their accompanying parent to the lab's playroom, where they informed parents of the study procedure. The appointment lasted approximately 45 minutes. After a familiarisation period in the playroom, the experimenter guided the child and their parent to the study room, where the parent was asked to complete questionnaires on their demographic information, the child's language exposure, the child's Theory of Mind (irrelevant to the current study), and their own cultural values on a tablet. As previously mentioned, this study was part of a bigger project. Thus, the procedure started with a task measuring receptive vocabulary (BILEX; Gampe et al., 2018), followed by visual perspective-taking (Director's task; Agostini et al., 2024), and non-verbal cue understanding (Yow & Markman, 2011), which were counterbalanced in order. Then, the over-imitation task was administered. The tasks administered after the over-imitation task assessed inhibition and task-switching. If children were bilingual or bidialectal, they participated in a receptive vocabulary task in their other language at the end of the procedure. The over-imitation task was administered approximately midway through the procedure, so that the children were more familiar with the experimenter but not yet fatigued.

The experimenter followed the same task procedure for each child.

The full procedure was recorded on video and coded afterwards. Upon completing each task in the procedure, the child earned a sticker for a sticker-collection card they received at the start of the appointment. The procedure of the over-imitation task is an adaptation from Schleihauf et al. (2018) and consists of only the "Transparent Tube Condition". It involves a modelling phase and a testing phase, and it does not include any manipulation of experimenter characteristics.

Over-imitation

Modelling Phase. The experimenter placed the transparent container on a table in front of the child, but angled towards herself, and took a seat on a chair next to the child. She asked the child to pay close attention, then performed a series of four redundant actions, before lifting the lid and obtaining the marble with the magnetic rod. The order of the action was standardised and the same across participants. The experimenter 1) clapped her hands three times, 2) pushed the lever from left to right and back, 3) tapped the magnetic rod in her left hand three times, and 4) used the back of the magnetic rod to push the black button. As classified by Schleihauf and Hoehl (2020), two of these actions were noncontact (steps 1 and 3; clapping and tapping), and two were pseudo-instrumental (steps 2 and 4; pushing the lever and the button). The experimenter then opened the lid, inserted the magnetic tip into the tube to retrieve the marble, and showed it to the child.

Testing Phase. After the modelling phase, the experimenter turned the transparent container towards the child and said: "Now it's your turn. You can do it however you want. You can't go wrong." (Swiss German: "Jetzt bisch du dra. Du chaschs eso mache, wie du möchtisch. Du chasch nüt falsch mache"). While the child interacted with the transparent container, the experimenter went to organise a cupboard, so as not to pressure the child by observing them. The experimenter turned around, towards the cupboard, her back and side towards the child, but did not leave the room. The child was therefore outside her field of view, and they could not see the experimenter's face. The over-imitation phase ended when the child signalled to the experimenter that they had got a marble out and confirmed that they were finished playing with the puzzle box. The full procedure was recorded on video. The procedure is openly available in Open Science Framework (OSF; at: https://osf.io/nfhms/overview?view_only=560c253e91b04401a9f1f75ea073162b [link for blind peer review, we will share the public link upon acceptance]).

Measures

Over-Imitation

Children's over-imitation was measured using the over-imitation task (see Procedure). A trained observer coded the over-imitation of each redundant action from video. They coded whether the child performed or attempted to perform (e.g., clapping once instead of three times) the action during the testing phase (as "1") or not (as "0") in a spreadsheet. A second trained observer coded the videos from 30 children (23% of the sample) using the same procedure. We computed inter-observer reliability using Cohen's Kappa for binary categories (action imitated vs. not). The kappa value was 0.93, indicating almost perfect (96.7%) agreement between coders (Landis & Koch, 1977). In case of disagreements between the observers, we used the values from the first observer, who coded the entire dataset. We differentiated between noncontact actions (actions that do not involve physical interaction with the transparent container, i.e., actions 1 and 3) and pseudo-instrumental actions (actions that do involve physical contact with the container, i.e., actions 2 and 4).

Language Status

Children's language status was measured using the Language Exposure questionnaire for Multilinguals Online (LEMON; https://www.quassel.ch/; Openscript GmbH, 2025). Parents were asked for the amount of time the child spends with each interaction partner and is exposed to each language/language variety for each caregiving situation since the child's birthday, for each day of the week, each interaction partner, and each language. We determined language status based on the amount of time the child is exposed to each language/language variety. All children in our sample were exposed to the societal language, Swiss German.

Parental Cultural Values

Parental cultural values were assessed using a digitalised version of the Global Leadership and Organizational Behaviour Effectiveness (GLOBE; House et al., 2004) survey, openly available through https://globeproject.com/data/GLOBE-Phase-2-Beta-Questionnaire-2006.pdf. The parent accompanying the child during the lab appointment completed the questionnaire during this visit. The questionnaire was subsequently sent to the other parent (if applicable) by email. The GLOBE consists of nine cultural dimensions: power orientation, in-group collectivism, gender egalitarianism, uncertainty avoidance, future orientation, institutional collectivism, performance orientation, humane orientation, and assertiveness. The scales describe "between-society" differences, see Table 1 for definitions of the cultural dimensions and S6 in the supplementary materials for the internal consistency on the dimensions.

[Insert Table 1 here] The questionnaire distinguishes between how the respondent perceives the society they reside in ("as is") versus how they believe a society should aspire to be ("should be"). The current study included only the "should be" values because all participants lived within the same society and therefore shared a common social context, making differences in parents' perceived cultural practices unlikely to be a major source of between-participant variance. In contrast, there is substantial individual variation in values about how a society should function, and perceptions of current social practices may not reflect the personal ideals that parents aspire to (Fischer & Boer, 2016; Fischer & Schwartz, 2011)." Should be" values, therefore, capture the cultural values children are exposed to through their parents more directly than parents' perceptions of the current societal norms. The subscale consists of 39 questions on a 7-point Likert scale. The final score is calculated as the mean score of both parents.

Cultural Diversity

To assess differences between parents' values, we calculated a Euclidean distance score (Carlier et al., 2024) based on their responses to the GLOBE questionnaire (House et al., 2004). Euclidean distance is widely used in multidimensional scaling and psychological research (Carlier et al., 2024). It aggregates discrepancies across multiple dimensions into a single continuous measure, giving greater weight to larger differences and capturing overall multidimensional divergence. For each cultural dimension, we first computed the difference between the two parents' scores and combined them into a single measure reflecting the overall discrepancy between parents' cultural values (D):

With n as the total number of assessed cultural dimensions, i as the answered cultural dimension, and x and y for the cultural values of parents 1 and 2 on this dimension.

Analysis

Our preregistered models included each different dimension of parental cultural values (analysed separately), age, action type and action step. Because the different steps were the same for all children (steps 1 and 3 were noncontact, and steps 2 and 4 were pseudo-instrumental), action type and action step in the model were collinear, which caused convergence problems. We, therefore, removed action type to obtain stable models and examined its effect through post-hoc contrasts computed on the posterior draws. Specifically, we compared the average estimate for steps 1 and 3 with the average estimate for steps 2 and 4. Because action step was sum-coded, the coefficient for step 4 was reconstructed as the negative sum of the coefficients for steps 1, 2, and 3. The planned contrast was therefore calculated as: ((step 1 + step 3) -(step 2 + step 4)) / 2. This contrast was computed for both the main effect of action step and the interaction between action step and the predictor of interest. The interaction contrast tested whether the association between the predictor and over-imitation differed between these two groups of action steps. For full model parameters, see Table S1 in supplementary materials. It should be noted that action step and action type are not equivalent. Whilst they were collinear, action step additionally captures variance that may be attributed to presentation order and working memory demands. The post-hoc contrasts for action type should therefore be interpreted with caution, as step-related factors cannot be fully disentangled from action-type effects.

We analysed our data using Bayesian Generalised Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs). Because the outcome variable was binary (the action was either imitated or not), we modelled it with a Bernoulli distribution. We used random intercepts for each child to account for repeated measurements across action steps. The nine models on parental cultural values had the following structure: over-imitation ∼ score on dimension of parental cultural values * action step (4 levels) + age + (1|child). We analysed the effect of cultural diversity with the following model: over-imitation ∼ cultural diversity * action step (4 levels) + age + (1|child), and the effect of language status with the following model: over-imitation ∼ language status (3 levels) * action step (4 levels) + age + (1|child). All models were fitted using the brms package (Bürkner, 2017) in R (R Core Team, 2025). We standardised all predictors to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. We contrast-coded all categorical predictors to sum up to a mean of 1. We used weakly informative priors for the fixed effects of interest being norm(0, 1), norm(0, 10) for age, and the default norm prior provided by the brms package (Bürkner, 2017) for action step. We used probability of direction (pd) as our reference index (Makowski et al., 2019) for the fixed effects and accepted our hypothesis if the pd >= 90%. The full analysis code used in this study is publicly available on the OSF, as detailed in the Data Availability Statement.

Results

We excluded 5 children from the final analysis for the following reasons: interference of the parent during the procedure (n = 1, monolingual boy), familiarity with the task (n = 1, monolingual boy), not wanting to participate in the task (n = 2, one monolingual and one bilingual boy), and missing data from the GLOBE questionnaire (n = 1, bidialectal girl). Further, we excluded another 8 children from the analyses containing language status, because they did not fulfil the inclusion criterion regarding language exposure. From the analyses containing cultural diversity, we excluded 23 children, because the GLOBE questionnaire was completed by only one parent, and cultural diversity could therefore not be calculated. See Table S5 for the sample characteristics for each model.

On average, children imitated 1.94 (SD = 1.23) out of 4 actions. Noncontact actions were less likely to be imitated (M = 0.61, SD = 0.72) than pseudo-instrumental actions (M = 1.33, SD = 0.81; Median β = -2.24, 89%CI[-2.70, -1.82], pd = 100%), see Figure 2. For the descriptive statistics on all nine dimensions of the GLOBE questionnaire and the Euclidean distance between parents, see Table S4.

[Insert Figure 2 here] Parental institutional collectivism was negatively associated with children's over-imitation behaviour (Median β = -0.29, 89%CI[-0.59, 0.01], pd = 93.90%), regardless of action type (pd < 90%). Children from parents who endorsed more institutionally collectivistic values were less likely to over-imitate, regardless of whether the actions were pseudo-instrumental or noncontact, see Figure 3.

[Insert Figure 3 here] The preceding analysis of institutional collectivism constituted our single confirmatory hypothesis. All remaining analyses, including parental in-group collectivism reported next, were exploratory and should be interpreted accordingly.

These analyses showed the following results, see also [Insert Figure 4 here] The cultural diversity of children's environment interacted with action step (Median β = 0.90, 89%CI[0.44, 1.37], pd = 99.98%). Pseudo-instrumental, but not noncontact actions, were less likely to be imitated by children whose parents reported larger differences in cultural values, see Figure 5.

Children's language status was not associated with their over-imitation behaviour (pd < 90%). Further, we analysed whether a family's language status predicted the difference in cultural values between parents. We did not find evidence of an association between language status and cultural differences (pd < 90%). To check whether our measure of cultural diversity was sensitive enough to detect the different variability between couples, we conducted a non-preregistered analysis in which we compared the Euclidean distances within couples to those calculated between any pair of parents. The model showed that the Euclidean distance in couples was smaller than in any random pair (Median β = 0.21, 89%CI[0.08, 0.35], pd = 99.60%), meaning that couples show smaller differences in their cultural values than randomly compared individuals.

Discussion

This study investigated the relationship between parental cultural values, the difference between them (as a proxy for cultural diversity), language status, and children's over-imitation of redundant pseudo-instrumental and noncontact actions. We recruited 3.5 to 4.5-year-olds from a wider Zurich area. The sample came from families with a predominantly high SES. Children observed an adult experimenter performing redundant actions on a transparent puzzle box before removing a marble from it. They were then given the opportunity to interact with the puzzle box themselves. Overall, children over-imitated pseudo-instrumental actions more often than noncontact actions. This is in line with previous findings (Clay et al., 2018) and the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020). Language status was not associated with children's over-imitation. Parental institutional collectivism was negatively associated with children's over-imitation, regardless of action type. The pattern of relationships between parental cultural values on several other dimensions was complex, with some dimensions showing a main effect (e.g., performance orientation), and others interacting with action type (e.g., in-group collectivism or power distance). The distance between parental cultural values across all dimensions, used as a proxy for cultural diversity in children's environment, also interacted with the action type. Pseudo-instrumental, but not noncontact actions, were less likely to be imitated by children whose parents differed more in their cultural values. These relationships could not be explained by children's language status, because parental cultural values did not differ between monolingual, bilingual and bidialectal children. To sum up, parental cultural values, but not children's language status, influenced children's over-imitation of redundant actions.

Parental Cultural Values

Contrary to our hypothesis, parental institutional collectivism was negatively associated with over-imitation, regardless of action type. This suggests that children of parents with stronger institutional collectivist values were less likely to reproduce redundant actions overall. As defined above, these two dimensions operate at different levels of social organisation. Institutional collectivism concerns societal-level collective action, whereas in-group collectivism reflects loyalty and cohesion within families and social groups. In line with the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020), we expected cultural dimensions would be associated with children's over-imitation of noncontact, but not pseudo-instrumental, actions, because these actions trigger deliberate considerations of whether or not to copy. We based our predictions for the dimension of institutional collectivism on the work of Gampe and Daum (2018). They found that bicultural children of parents with higher values of institutional collectivism intervened less saliently (more implicitly) when responding to norm violations. The authors suggested that higher institutional collectivism implies stronger group loyalty and less enforcement of norms on an individual level. Accordingly, we hypothesised that higher degrees of group loyalty would lead to higher levels of over-imitation of noncontact actions because children would apply the perceived norms by imitating them.

One possible explanation is that institutional collectivistic values guide parents' behaviour at a broader, systemic level, (e.g., "I believe that the economic system in this society should be designed to maximize (individual interests: 1; collective interests; 7)";

The Globe Foundation, 2006, p.15) and may therefore have a weaker impact on children's everyday social interactions. By contrast, in-group collectivistic values may shape caregiving styles (e.g., "Members of this society should (take no pride in being a member of the society: 1; take a great deal of pride in being a member of the society: 7)"; The Globe Foundation, 2006, p.18) and expectations for children's social behaviour (Gorla et al., 2024). These values may shape children's behaviour more directly toward conformity and affiliation and, consequently, could explain their greater imitation of redundant actions if they interpreted them as normative (Clegg & Legare, 2016). An alternative explanation concerns norm salience, rather than norm adherence. The link between higher institutional collectivism and less explicit responses to norm violations (Gampe & Daum, 2018) could reflect reduced individual-level norm enforcement, rather than stronger group loyalty. Children from higher institutional collectivism backgrounds may perceive norm enforcement as a collective or institutional responsibility, rather than a personal one. This may lead them to feel less compelled to over-imitate overtly.

In this case, lower over-imitation would reflect reduced individual norm salience rather than weaker normative motivations.

Exploratory analyses showed different patterns of associations between other dimensions of parental cultural values and children's over-imitation. Parental gender egalitarianism, assertiveness, power distance, and performance orientation were associated with children's over-imitation patterns, and showed both differences in imitation across action types and overall levels of over-imitation. The cultural dimensions humane orientation, future orientation, and uncertainty avoidance showed no associations with children's over-imitation. Because of the exploratory nature of these analyses, the results should be interpreted with caution, and any explanation for these associations is speculative.

Although exploratory, these findings are consistent with the previous findings showing the extent to which children over-imitate differs between cultures (Berl & Hewlett, 2015; Clegg & Legare, 2016; Fong et al., 2021; Nielsen & Tomaselli, 2010; Nielsen et al., 2014; Stengelin et al., 2019 Stengelin et al., , 2020)). Here, we recruited children living in the wider Zurich area in Switzerland, and we directly quantified the cultural values in children's environments that might have produced these differences, whereas previous research relied on contrasts between specific nations. Parents have an important impact on children's cultural values, but so do the cultural norms within the society where children are raised (Kalmijn, 2015). We did not measure prevalent societal values or how far the parents in our study deviated from or adhered to them, so we could not capture the entirety of the cultural environment of the children.

To sum up, parental in-group collectivism was positively associated with the over-imitation of both types of actions, possibly showing increased norm adherence in children of parents who endorse group loyalty and mutual dependence within families and social groups. However, the overall association between parental cultural values and their children's over-imitation varies per dimension of cultural values, which makes drawing general conclusions difficult. Further research could explore the full impact of children's cultural environment by examining both parental and societal values, the distance between them and their impact on over-imitation.

Cultural Diversity

In addition to specific cultural dimensions influencing children's over-imitation, we found that the distance between parents' cultural values across the nine value dimensions was associated with children's over-imitation of pseudo-instrumental actions only. Children whose parents had low differences in cultural values over-imitated pseudo-instrumental actions more than children whose parents had high differences, but their over-imitation of noncontact actions was comparable. Children who grow up in homes with divergent cultural values may encounter more normative ambiguity in daily life. This may increase their sensitivity to behaviours with unclear causal function, which in turn may prompt deliberate consideration of whether or not to copy (type 2 processing). Pseudo-instrumental actions could be particularly subject to this, as their causal irrelevance is less clear than for noncontact actions. Bicultural households show greater flexibility in norm-related judgments (Iannuccilli et al., 2021) and develop more nuanced strategies for interpreting ambiguous social information (Kalmijn, 2015).

Children from culturally diverse households may therefore be more used to causal ambiguity, which pseudo-instrumental actions can cause. This contrasts with the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020), which predicts blanket copying rather than deliberate consideration for pseudo-instrumental actions. However, all explanations are speculative, given the exploratory nature of this analysis, but they present a promising avenue for future research.

Quantifying the cultural diversity children grow up in is worthwhile, as it captures a source of diversity in children's environments that remains masked when averaging the scores across parents. Moreover, children may have parents with identical mean cultural scores, yet have fundamentally different experiences in their home environments. This ranges from growing up with parents with the same cultural backgrounds to parents with completely opposite cultural values. Parental cultural values, however, are only one of the influential components in children's cultural environments. Children receive cultural input from caregivers beyond their parents or primary caregivers, such as peers (Rogoff, 1981) or teachers in educational settings (Scheidecker et al., 2023). Childcare teachers, for example, carry cultural beliefs about developmental goals and collaboration affecting their teaching practices (van Schaik et al., 2014). This is relevant, given that most cross-cultural research assumes homogeneous environments (Smith & Bond, 2019), which overlooks the diversity that children experience in their everyday lives (Padilla, 2008; Yulianto, 2023). However, capturing the cultural values of everyone in children's lives presents a methodological challenge. The current study's contribution of capturing the cultural values of both caregivers, and quantifying the distance between them, is a first step in that direction.

Development of the Dual-Processes

One possible explanation for our findings is that, in the present age group, pseudo-instrumental actions may be more likely to trigger type 2 processing than the non-contact actions. Because the children in our sample were of preschool age and younger than those in most previous studies (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020), they may not have fully developed the blanket copying heuristic yet (McGuigan & Whiten, 2009), and relied on type 2 processing instead. Evidence suggests that infants already show deliberate consideration of whether to copy others' actions (Gergely & Csibra, 2003; Gergely et al., 2002), but see also Beisert et al. (2012) and Paulus et al. (2011) for alternative explanations. If blanket copying has not been fully developed, neither action type should then elicit type 1 processing. This would mean that both types of actions elicit type 2 processing, triggering deliberate considerations on whether or not to copy.

In turn, factors such as culture (Clegg & Legare, 2016; Fong et al., 2021) or social or normative goals (Hoehl et al., 2019) could influence this. In addition, children's perception of causal relevance to object-bound actions could explain that preschool children copy object-focused (pseudo-instrumental) actions more than older children (Clay et al., 2018). With age, children's focus shifts from their assumptions about causality to social (Nielsen & Blank, 2011) and normative (Kenward, 2012) context of the demonstration. As the current sample consisted of children between 3.5 to 4.5 years of age, children were likely to consider copying actions based on their possible causal relevance. This account, however, does not explain why the two action types showed different patterns of association with cultural variables. If both elicit type 2 processing, both should be susceptible to cultural influence, yet this was not what we observed.

We used a transparent puzzle box, which could have made the children realise that the pseudo-instrumental actions were not causally relevant (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020; Schleihauf et al., 2018), thereby making it more likely that type 2 processing would be triggered. Furthermore, the social context of the task may have shaped children's motivation for imitation because imitation serves both instrumental and social communicative functions (Over & Carpenter, 2013; Uzgiris, 1981). Besides learning about an object, children may copy behaviour to communicate social alignment. In this study's procedure, however, after demonstrating the action sequence, the experimenter disengaged from the child and turned to another activity, while the child interacted with the puzzle box to retrieve the marble. This design choice may have reduced the child's social-communicative motivation, as they did not interact with the experimenter during the puzzle box task. Children's copying behaviour may, therefore, have been primarily driven by instrumental rather than affiliative goals. As a result, children may have disregarded noncontact actions that were clearly redundant immediately. In contrast, pseudo-instrumental actions may have elicited deliberate consideration, which showed association with parents' cultural values and the cultural diversity in the home environment. Because of children's focus on the object and the nature of the task, we suggest that type 2 processing could have been elicited for the pseudo-instrumental actions. Working memory may have modulated this process as well, given that actions demonstrated later (steps 3 and 4) were more likely to be reproduced than those demonstrated earlier (steps 1 and 2), for both noncontact and pseudo-instrumental actions. This suggests that the retention and deliberate consideration of whether or not to copy actions could depend partly on children's working memory capacity as well (Rusnak et al., 2022; Speidel et al., 2021). Because we did not measure working memory in this study, this remains speculative. Individual differences in parents' cultural values and the cultural diversity of the home environment may, therefore, be more likely to shape children's imitation patterns of pseudo-instrumental actions or all actions equally, a pattern we found for several individual dimensions of parental cultural values as well.

The present findings suggest that the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020) could be refined to solve the tension noted above. Rather than assuming both action types elicit type 2 processing, responses to causally irrelevant actions may vary along a continuum depending on how readily their irrelevance can be detected.

The current framework distinguishes between type 1 blanket copying, triggered by causally ambiguous actions, and type 2 deliberate considerations, triggered when causal irrelevance is recognised. The present results, however, suggest that causally irrelevant actions could be conceptualised along a continuum, depending on how readily the causal irrelevance can be detected. When causal irrelevance is highly salient (i.e., with noncontact actions), children may dismiss the action automatically, without deliberation, resulting in low copying, regardless of cultural or contextual factors (blanket non-copying), similar to type 1 processing but in the opposite direction. When causal irrelevance is moderately ambiguous (i.e., with pseudo-instrumental actions), children may deliberately consider whether or not to copy, which could be influenced by cultural and contextual factors. When causal irrelevance is very hard to detect, children may blankly copy. In addition, how easy it is to detect the causal irrelevance could also vary with age, consistent with previous findings (Clay et al., 2018). Such a continuum represents the current findings more cleanly than the proposed dual-process framework and could guide future research into the conditions under which each mode of processing is activated. The association between parental cultural values and children's over-imitation is consistent with a normative account of the dual-process Perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020). Higher parental in-group collectivism was associated with greater over-imitation, suggesting that children of parents who endorse group loyalty and mutual dependence within families or social groups may have stronger normative motivations to copy the demonstrated actions. The aligns with previous cross-cultural findings showing that children from more collectivistic backgrounds over-imitate more, which is attributed to greater norm-conformity (Clegg & Legare, 2016; Fong et al., 2021). However, normative processes may not be the only mechanism through which culture shapes over-imitation. Cultural values may equally affect children's instrumental or affiliative goals (Hoehl et al., 2019). Children from certain cultural backgrounds may be more motivated to learn from demonstrated actions for instrumental reasons, or may copy actions to signal social alignment with the experimenter. These processes could also contribute to the pattern of associations we observed between parental cultural values and children's over-imitation we observed.

Neither a purely normative nor a purely instrumental or affiliative account fully explains why the influence of parental cultural values and cultural diversity was stronger for pseudo-instrumental than noncontact actions, contrary to the predictions of the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020). Disentangling these mechanisms would require study designs that explicitly manipulate the framing of the task by, for example, presenting actions as either normative or instrumental (Clay et al., 2018; Keupp et al., 2013) or by introducing conditions on the experimenter's presence during the testing phase (Nielsen & Blank, 2011). If children's cultural environments shape their over-imitation through normative motivations, effects should become apparent in normative framings and when the experimenter is present. If cultural environments shape children's over-imitation through cognitive processes, no differences should be observed between the framings or in absence or presence of the experimenter.

One unexplored avenue in this line of research is the possibility that culture can affect children's over-imitation by influencing their cognition. A large body of previous research (e.g., Chiao, 2018; Kuwabara & Smith, 2012; Saxe & de Kirby, 2014) explains how culture can affect children's cognitive development, for instance, what they attend to during an event and what they learn from it (Qi & Roberts, 2019), and their socio-cognitive development (Kärtner et al., 2020). Based on our findings, future research should examine which mechanisms, normative or cognitive, are behind the effects of children's cultural environment on their over-imitation. For instance, by framing all actions as either normative or instrumental (Clay et al., 2018; Keupp et al., 2013) or having the researcher present or absent (Nielsen & Blank, 2011). If children's cultural environment affects their over-imitation through its impact on children's normative motivations, it should affect children's behaviour in the normative, but not instrumental framing, and in the presence of the researcher. If it affects children's over-imitation by influencing their cognitive processes when they observe the action demonstration, then the framing or presence of the researcher should have no influence on their behaviour. The results from such research could be used to further expand the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020) and other theoretical perspectives on over-imitation to encompass the full range of cultural effects.

Language Status

Growing up with more than one culture often comes with learning more than one language. Here, we did not find evidence that children's language status (i.e., being monolingual, bilingual, or bidialectal) affected their over-imitation, regardless of the action type. All children over-imitated both action types at similar levels. The fact that parents of bilingual or bidialectal children did not exhibit larger differences in cultural values than parents of monolingual children might explain this finding. As we could still show that partners have more cultural values in common than randomly paired people, it is unlikely that low sensitivity of our cultural diversity measures causes this pattern of results. Therefore, parents in our study had largely homogeneous cultural values, despite, at least for some of them, coming from different cultural backgrounds. Because we did not collect data on the parents' country of origin, some parents may have been either second-or third-generation immigrants (and thus assimilated into Swiss culture), or are from a different part of the country, e.g., French-or Italian-speaking. Therefore, bilingual children in our study (and in the general population in Switzerland) can, but do not have to be, bicultural as well. This highlights the need to measure children's cultural environment when investigating the effects of bilingualism on children's social behaviour. Bilinguals are a very heterogeneous group (Wermelinger et al., 2024), and without the measurement of the different sources of variability in their environment, the results of one study finding a difference between monolinguals and bilinguals might not generalise to other bilingual populations (Byers-Heinlein et al., 2019).

Methodological Considerations

The current study offers several strengths by exploring different factors that explain children's over-imitation behaviour, building on and expanding the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020). However, some methodological limitations should be noted. First, the use of the GLOBE questionnaire (House et al., 2004) to assess parents' cultural values imposes conceptual constraints, as the questionnaire was originally developed to assess culture and value orientations in leadership and workplace contexts, rather than at the level of individual parents or family interactions (House et al., 2004 (House et al., , 2014)). Although GLOBE measures have been adapted for use with individuals (Gampe & Daum, 2018; Gorla et al., 2024), the connection between the GLOBE dimensions and individual-level caregiving practices remains unknown. As a result, the present analyses are exploratory, and the findings should be interpreted as identifying associations rather than providing evidence for causal relationships. The current results highlight the need for future research into different dimensions of culture, parents' cultural values, and ways to measure these at the family-level in caregiving contexts. Second, it is worth noting that GLOBE's definition of in-group collectivism emphasises loyalty and group pride relevant in the context of leadership and workplace contexts, which is different from how collectivism in conceptualised in the broader literature, which focuses more strongly on interdependence, social obligation, and conformity (Hofstede, 2001; Triandis, 2018). Furthermore, the experimental design minimised normative and social cues during both Modelling and Testing phases. After demonstrating the action sequence, the experimenter disengaged while the child interacted with the puzzle box. While this approach allowed for the assessment of children's spontaneous copying of redundant actions, it may have reduced social pressure and communicative motivation for imitation (Kenward et al., 2011; Legare & Nielsen, 2015; Over & Carpenter, 2013). This methodological decision may have shifted children's focus toward instrumental interpretations of actions rather than to social affiliation or norm adherence (Legare et al., 2015). As noted above, actions presented later were more likely to be reproduced (steps 3 and 4 vs. steps 1 and 2), consistent with a memory account and suggesting that step-related variance is real and non-trivial (see ??). Future studies should counterbalance the order of noncontact and pseudo-instrumental actions to disentangle these effects cleanly. Although these methodological constraints in this study prevented us from exploring the mechanisms underlying the influence of parental cultural values on children's over-imitation, the findings open a new research avenue.

Conclusion

The present study indicates that how preschool children over-imitate is associated with parental cultural values. 4-year-old children over-imitated pseudo-instrumental actions more than noncontact actions, highlighting their object-directed orientation at this developmental stage. The pattern of associations of several dimensions of parental cultural values to children's over-imitation was complex.

Contrary to the predictions of the dual-process perspective (Schleihauf & Hoehl, 2020), children's cultural environment was associated with their over-imitation of pseudo-instrumental actions more than noncontact actions. These results suggest that preschool children do not yet apply blanket copying to pseudo-instrumental actions, or that culture has an effect above and beyond children's normative motivation to over-imitate, and rather shapes how they process and learn from social interactions.

Rather than a binary distinction between blanket copying and deliberate consideration, responses to causally irrelevant actions may vary along a continuum of how readily the irrelevance can be detected. Highly salient irrelevance may produce blanket non-copying, moderate ambiguity may trigger deliberate consideration, which could be influenced by cultural factors, and low salience of irrelevance may produce blanket copying.

Overall, this study suggests that children's over-imitation is shaped not only by the properties of the demonstrated actions but also by the children's cultural environments, highlighting the importance of integrating individual cultural contexts into theories on social learning. review and editing. Table S6 Cronbach's Alpha per Cultural Dimension of the GLOBE Questionnaire Cultural Dimension Cronbach's α Institutional Collectivism 0.49 Assertiveness 0.55 Gender Egalitarianism 0.39 Performance Orientation 0.67 In-Group Collectivism 0.49 Power Distance 0.59 Uncertainty Avoidance 0.57 Humane Orientation 0.67 Future Orientation 0.53 may operate on both the contextual and the individual level, influencing how children interpret contextual cues as well as which goals they pursue.

The current study focuses on the individual factors that might influence children's over-imitation, specifically children's cultural background.

Figure 4. Parental assertiveness interacted with action type (Median β = -0.49, 89%CI[-0.90, -0.07], pd = 97.17%). Higher assertiveness was associated with children's increased imitation of pseudo-instrumental actions, but not of noncontact actions. Similarly, parental gender egalitarianism interacted with action type (Median β = 0.55, 89%CI[0.13, 0.96], pd = 98.45%). Children of parents reporting lower gender egalitarianism imitated more pseudo-instrumental than noncontact actions. In contrast, children of parents reporting higher gender egalitarianism imitated both action types equally. Parental performance orientation showed a main effect on over-imitation (Median β = 0.22, 89%CI[-0.05, 0.51], pd = 90.65%). Higher parental performance orientation was associated to a greater likelihood of children imitating the observed actions, regardless of action type. Parental in-group collectivism was positively associated with over-imitation (Median β = 0.27, 89%CI[-0.02, 0.58], pd = 93.03%), predicting children's increased over-imitation regardless of action type. Parental power distance interacted with action type (Median β = -0.36, 89%CI[-0.76, 0.03], pd = 92.77%), with children of parents reporting lower power distance showing similar imitation frequencies across action types, whereas children of parents reporting higher power distance exhibited larger differences. We did not find supporting evidence for any effect of the cultural dimensions of uncertainty avoidance, humane orientation, and future orientation in parents on over-imitation in children (all pd < 90%).
